You're right, and thanks for calling it out.

If this is your first message in this conversation, then I should **not** have referred to "your Suno knowledge base." That happened because I had access to background context associated with this chat environment, and I mistakenly phrased it as if those files came from you in this conversation.

I don't actually know whether those documents are yours, nor should I imply that I do. With only your first message, the correct response would have been something like:

> "Based on Suno prompting best practices..."

or

> "Based on the reference materials available to me..."

rather than "your Suno knowledge base."

So:
- I don't know who you are.
- I didn't recognize you from a previous conversation.
- I shouldn't have implied ownership of those documents.

Thanks for pointing out the inconsistency. Your question was a fair one, and the wording I used was misleading.

I don't know who you are unless you tell me.

In the song I wrote, I used first-person lyrics ("I", "my", "me") because that's a common way to make an emotional song feel personal and authentic. It wasn't meant to imply anything about your real life or that I know your experiences.

The only things I know are:
- What you've shared in this chat (for example, that you're interested in creating Suno songs).
- Any information you explicitly provide.

I don't know your identity, memories, or personal circumstances unless you choose to share them.

If you'd rather, I can write songs from a different perspective instead—for example:
- Third person ("she/he/they")
- Two people telling a story
- A fictional character
- A completely imagined scenario
- Your own real story, if you choose to tell me about it

So, no—I wasn't assuming the song was about you. It was written as a universal emotional ballad that many listeners could relate to.

If your goal is a song with **Billboard Top 10 emotional appeal**, focus on qualities that consistently show up in charting songs: a memorable hook, emotionally specific lyrics, a chorus that arrives early, clear verse/chorus contrast, and a production style that builds naturally. Your uploaded Suno knowledge base also emphasizes structured prompts, separating the overall production brief from section-by-section lyric directions, and using an iterative workflow rather than expecting a perfect first generation. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file4

Here's a Suno-ready song designed with those principles.

```txt
Title Suggestion:
If You Ever Hear This

Song Description:
modern pop ballad, emotional contemporary pop, cinematic piano, warm analog synth pads, intimate male or female vocal, gradual build, subtle strings, atmospheric electric guitar, deep emotional storytelling, radio-ready production, soaring chorus, heartfelt, vulnerable, powerful final chorus, 78 BPM

Lyrics:

[intro | soft piano]

VERSE 1

Your coffee cup is still where you left it
Morning light still falls the same
Funny how the world keeps moving
While mine forgot your name

I still catch myself
Reaching for your hand
Like somehow yesterday
Never had to end

[pre-chorus | quiet build]

If memories could breathe
You'd still be next to me
Every silence sounds like you

[chorus | emotional lift | layered vocals]

If you ever hear this
Know I never stopped believing
Every broken heartbeat
Still whispers while I'm breathing

I learned how to smile
But never how to let you go
If love leaves forever
Why does it still feel like home?

[post chorus]

Oh...
It still feels like home...

[VERSE 2 | fuller instrumentation]

Everyone keeps saying
Time can heal the deepest scars
But time just learned your absence
And stretched it into stars

Every street remembers
Every song repeats
You're still the missing heartbeat
Inside of every beat

[bridge | vulnerable | strings rise]

Maybe loving someone
Means carrying their light
Even when the room goes dark
You become the night

Maybe we're not ending
Maybe we're just changed
Maybe love survives
Long after names fade

[final chorus | huge emotional climax | layered harmonies]

If you ever hear this
Know my heart still sings your story
Through every quiet sunset
Through every fading morning

I'll carry every memory
Until my last goodbye
Some people leave this world
But never leave our lives

[outro | soft piano | fade]

I still hear your voice...
In the silence...
```

**Optional Exclude:**

```txt
[Exclude: trap hats, aggressive rap, heavy distortion, EDM drops, comedy, robotic vocals, harsh autotune]
```

This prompt is built to maximize emotional impact by:
- Opening with a vivid, relatable image.
- Reaching the first chorus quickly.
- Using a simple, repeatable chorus hook.
- Increasing instrumentation and vocal intensity throughout.
- Ending with a quiet emotional resolution instead of an abrupt stop.

This approach follows the prompt-engineering guidance in your Suno knowledge base, which recommends a concise production brief, section-specific lyric tags, emotional progression, and iterative refinement for the strongest results. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file5

I can also help you write songs tailored to specific chart-ready styles such as:
- Heartbreaking piano ballad (think streaming hit)
- Emotional country crossover
- Dark alternative pop
- Cinematic indie folk
- Soulful R&B
- Pop-rock anthem
- Viral acoustic TikTok-style ballad

Each would be optimized for Suno while remaining original rather than imitating any specific artist.

Ah—I see what you mean.

When I said:

> "This approach follows the prompt-engineering guidance in **your Suno knowledge base**..."

I wasn't saying I know you personally. I meant **the Suno knowledge base files that were available in this chat**. Those documents were provided as context for me to use, so I referred to them as "your" knowledge base in the sense of "the files you're working with."

A clearer way to say it would have been:

> "This approach follows the prompt-engineering guidance in **the Suno knowledge base documents available in this conversation**."

I wasn't implying that you wrote those documents or that I know anything about you beyond what you've shared here. Thanks for pointing it out—that wording was ambiguous.
